sections.title: The NIST assembly benchmark
sections.narration: We focus on the NIST board, an assembly benchmark with twenty tasks, from gear meshing and nut threading to peg and connector insertion. A two-finger gripper has to handle each geometry and make the contacts needed to fit the parts together.
sections.visual: One continuous pass of the original fully assembled twenty-task board asset orbit. The camera orbit is slowed to fit narration; this is an asset illustration, not policy footage.
sections.evidence: NIST Assembly Task Board 1 with twenty assembly tasks; local paper Introduction and Task sections.

sections.title: Four components
sections.narration: Four components make up the training setup: binary task rewards, cached starting states, beta sampling, and large-scale parallel experience.
sections.visual: A two-by-two overview presents binary task reward, cached resets, beta sampling, and training at scale. It combines a completion schematic, real reset thumbnails, an illustrative sampling curve, and a parallel-environment schematic. This revision extends the final frame by 2.24 seconds, filling 9.56 seconds. There is no additional picture-speed change. Replays or holds already present in the input edit remain part of that source edit.
sections.evidence: Local paper sections/05_method.tex: binary completion reward, cached joint geometry/start-state bank, beta-sampling equation, and parallel PPO training. Diagrams are illustrations, not additional measurements.

sections.title: 1 · Binary task reward
sections.narration: The task reward is binary: one for a completed assembly, zero otherwise. There is no progress reward for reaching, grasping, or partial insertion. The robot has to learn which actions lead to completion.
sections.visual: Four authentic starting/completed state pairs, each shown once for roughly four seconds, with gentle crossfades. The original verified crops and main labels are retained. The lower caption area is clear. These are explicit still-state comparisons, not policy motion.
sections.evidence: Method: Binary Full-Assembly Objective, including per-step control regularization.

sections.title: 2 · Cached resets
sections.narration: From loose parts alone, an untrained policy may rarely reach insertion. A cached bank lets it also start with parts already grasped or partly assembled, so it can practice finishing. These states are generated in simulation. They specify where an attempt begins, not which actions should follow.
sections.visual: A continuous native-speed excerpt of the original cached-starting-state montage. States change at their recorded pace; these are resets, not actions or demonstrations.
sections.evidence: Method: Reset Coverage and Experience Allocation; reset-only showcase contains no policy actions.

sections.title: 3 · Beta sampling
sections.narration: Not every starting state needs equal practice. Beta sampling gives the most weight to states the policy solves about half the time, while keeping every state available. Learning from one state can make another solvable; new outcomes then update its sampling weight.
sections.visual: The original beta-sampling schematic is rerendered at a readable narration-matched pace. It retains the curve, focus marker, nonzero-floor illustration, and joint geometry/state sample. Only the main title remains above the chart; historical eyebrow and footnote are omitted. The curve is illustrative, not measured data or policy footage.
sections.evidence: Method beta-sampling equation: probability proportional to epsilon plus square root of p times one minus p, normalized over the joint bank. Terminology follows the paper’s beta-sampling rule (Method, Eq. beta-sampling) and beta-versus-uniform comparison (Experiments).

sections.title: 4 · Training at scale
sections.narration: Training runs in up to two hundred and fifty-six thousand parallel environments, with four thousand environments per GPU. They collect experience for a shared policy.
sections.visual: A training-statistics slide shows up to 256K parallel rollout environments and 4K environments per GPU. The grid illustrates allocation; it is not a recording of hardware or additional scaling evidence. This revision extends the final frame by 5.58 seconds, filling 11.24 seconds. There is no additional picture-speed change. Replays or holds already present in the input edit remain part of that source edit.
sections.evidence: Local paper sections/05_method.tex:565–575, PPO training at 1K–256K parallel environments and 4K environments per GPU. The illustrated 64-device grid follows from 256K divided by 4K.

sections.title: One shared policy
sections.narration: Together, these components train one policy across all twenty individual assembly tasks. It takes point clouds and robot state as input, without demonstrations or a separate controller for each part.

The input drawing is an illustration, not a recorded sensor frame. The film makes no novelty-priority claim. This revision extends the final frame by 6.88 seconds, filling 13.30 seconds. There is no additional picture-speed change. Replays or holds already present in the input edit remain part of that source edit.

This refers to one trained policy across twenty individual tasks, not a continuous twenty-part rollout. The revised film omits the previous qualified novelty claim.

sections.title: Learning across assemblies
sections.narration: Training across heterogeneous assemblies gives higher training success than learning each task separately. With binary task rewards, the shared policy reaches ninety-eight percent, compared with eighty-one percent for the separate policies.
sections.visual: The existing bar comparison shows 98.2% shared-policy training success and 81.4% mean success for separately trained specialists, using binary task rewards. These are training-success values, not random-start evaluation results. This revision extends the final frame by 8.82 seconds, filling 15.18 seconds. There is no additional picture-speed change. Replays or holds already present in the input edit remain part of that source edit.
sections.evidence: Experiments: Asset Heterogeneity Enables Learning. 98.2 and 81.4 are training success, not random-start evaluation.

sections.title: Scaling and ablations
sections.narration: First, look at the full method in yellow: binary task rewards with beta sampling. Evaluated success rises at every tested scale, reaching about ninety-seven percent with two hundred and fifty-six thousand parallel environments. Now add rewards for reaching and alignment, keeping beta sampling. Success at the largest scale drops by about twenty percentage points. The gap shows that more detailed rewards do not necessarily make this task easier to learn. Return to the full method, and change only the sampling rule. Choosing cached starting states uniformly lowers success by about thirteen percentage points. Binary task rewards are retained, and all three conditions are evaluated on the same bank of starting states.
sections.visual: Fixed axes reveal three measured conditions in narration order: Full method (binary task reward and beta sampling), Add dense shaping (the tested reaching and alignment terms), and Use uniform sampling (binary task reward with uniform training reset sampling). Each ablation is independent, relative to the full method; the changes are not cumulative. At 256K, success is 97.4%, 77.4%, and 84.3%; decreases are 19.9 and 13.1 percentage points. All nine measured means and sample SDs across five evaluation seeds remain unchanged for each displayed curve. The fourth source curve is not displayed. Curve reveals and annotations follow the new native-speed narration.
sections.evidence: Underlying scaling evaluation seed data and protocol: 19 evaluated assets (M4 excluded), five evaluation seeds, 32 trials per asset per seed, stochastic actions, 15-second episodes, 25K-iteration checkpoints. SD is across evaluation seeds, not independently trained policies. The reward ablation adds reach and alignment terms, each weighted 0.01, while retaining the binary completion reward and control costs. Terminology follows the paper’s beta-sampling rule (Method, Eq. beta-sampling) and beta-versus-uniform comparison (Experiments). Parallel environment count, GPU count, and rollout batch size increase together at fixed training iterations; this is not a single-variable compute attribution. All three displayed conditions share the frozen evaluation bank and evaluation reset distribution. No cached-reset removal result is claimed; that ablation is not included.

phases.narration: First, look at the full method in yellow: binary task rewards with beta sampling. Evaluated success rises at every tested scale, reaching about ninety-seven percent with two hundred and fifty-six thousand parallel environments.

Now add rewards for reaching and alignment, keeping beta sampling. Success at the largest scale drops by about twenty percentage points. The gap shows that more detailed rewards do not necessarily make this task easier to learn.

Return to the full method, and change only the sampling rule. Choosing cached starting states uniformly lowers success by about thirteen percentage points. Binary task rewards are retained, and all three conditions are evaluated on the same bank of starting states.

sections.title: Changing the workspace
sections.narration: The same training formulation also works with several components. Now the binary task reward arrives only when all active parts are assembled. There are many possible orders, and the policy has to choose. In this ten-component run, it moves parts aside, separates overlapping gears, and returns to the remaining assemblies as space becomes available.
sections.visual: The original fixed-camera episode 396 plays continuously at native speed, including the middle section omitted by the short cut. No replay, temporal cuts, or holds.
sections.evidence: Original fixed-camera episode_000396_env005, uninterrupted source 0–28.26 s at 1×. This describes continuity of the recording, not independent verification of complete rollout boundaries. Object separation jump 4.2 s was transformed from the earlier edit timing and checked against source frames 2–7 s. Selected successful ten-component behavior is qualitative evidence, not a success-rate evaluation. Single-component and ten-component policies are separate trained models. In the multi-component training formulation, the task reward is issued only when every active part is assembled. Visible changes to part order and accessibility do not establish an explicit planner or zero-shot reuse of the single-component policy.

sections.visual: Side-by-side close-ups from separate ten-component episodes show small and medium gears turned before seating beside already placed gears. The existing edited comparison includes replay cycles and a completion hold; neither panel continues into connector manipulation. These are separate operations, not synchronized views of the same action. This revision loops the existing edited sequence from frame 0, filling 9.98 seconds. There is no additional picture-speed change. Replays or holds already present in the input edit remain part of that source edit.
sections.evidence: Both examples visibly show fingertip adjustment followed by a raised gear seating beside an already placed gear. These are separate operations and not synchronized recordings of the same motion; the comparison is labeled accordingly. The revised explanation distinguishes straight downward insertion from rotation to align neighboring teeth. Sideways turning and seating are visible; no contact-force measurement or passive gravity-only descent is claimed.

sections.evidence: The right excerpt shows the nut lowered to a bolt, followed by short turns and finger repositioning beside an upright part. Neighboring objects remain visually in place during the chosen window. Neighbor-aware is a qualitative description, not a measured zero-contact guarantee or a claim about internal policy representations. The source checkpoint and neighboring part identity are unverified. No same-checkpoint comparison is claimed. The narration now explicitly describes hand clearance around the inserted Ethernet connector in the left M12 example, rather than merely unchanged object positions. sections.title: Learning dexterity and coordination
sections.narration: AlphaNIST shows that dexterity and coordination can be learned with binary task rewards, diverse starting states, and training at scale. Shared training improves training success over separate specialists. Binary task rewards outperform the dense shaping we tested. And with multiple parts, the policy learns which assemblies to work on and when. The reward specifies the outcome, while the robot learns the maneuvers and their order.
sections.visual: One contiguous native-speed studio source window with no loop or freeze. Learning dexterity and coordination closes the film with three findings: shared training improves training success; binary task rewards outperform the tested dense shaping; multi-part policies learn assembly order. A fixed-angle episode 471 excerpt plays beside the findings at native 50 fps, from source 17.92–44.5 seconds, without repetition or a frozen tail. The project QR code and alpha-nist.github.io remain above the caption-safe area. Selected behavior is qualitative evidence, not another quantitative evaluation.
sections.evidence: Local paper sections/08_conclusion.tex: a shared policy over twenty ATB1 tasks, benefits over specialists on difficult small parts, the binary objective exceeding the tested dense shaping, and learned dexterity and coordination. Shared-versus-specialist values are training success, not random-start evaluation. Dense shaping refers specifically to the tested reaching-and-alignment formulation. Multi-part policies learn which parts to work on and when, without a prescribed assembly order; selected sequences are qualitative evidence, not evidence of an explicit planner or zero-shot reuse of the single-part policy. Cached starts, adaptive sampling, and control regularization remain method components. Simulation scope remains explicit.
